10	## Purpose
11	
12	`src/server/services/auth-service.ts` owns credential registration, login, logout, and
13	password reset — no third-party identity provider is involved anywhere in this corpus.
14	`src/server/services/session-service.ts` owns the opaque session token lifecycle and the
15	bridge from a resolved session to a per-organization `Actor`. The two are sequential, not
16	peers: a successful `login` in `auth-service.ts` calls straight into
17	`session-service.ts`'s `createSessionToken` to mint the credential the browser actually keeps.
18	
19	What neither service owns: reading or writing the session cookie itself — REQ-206's "only one
20	module reads or writes the session cookie" names `src/lib/session.ts`, a module neither
21	service imports; both work entirely in terms of a bare token string or a `SessionPrincipal`
22	value, leaving the browser boundary to the caller.
23	
24	## Public surface
25	
26	| function | signature | permission action | events emitted | errors thrown |
27	|---|---|---|---|---|
28	| `register` | `(input: RegisterInput) => Promise<{ user: User; org: Organization }>` | none | none (see DES-164) | plain `Error` (email taken) |
29	| `login` | `(input: LoginInput) => Promise<{ user: User; token: string }>` | none | none | plain `Error` (rate limit, bad credentials) |
30	| `logout` | `(sessionId: SessionId) => Promise<void>` | none | none | none |
31	| `requestPasswordReset` | `(input: PasswordResetRequestInput) => Promise<void>` | none | none | none (always resolves) |
32	| `confirmPasswordReset` | `(input: PasswordResetConfirmInput) => Promise<User>` | none | none | plain `Error` (rate limit, invalid token) |
33	| `createSessionToken` | `(userId: UserId) => Promise<{ token: string; expiresAt: IsoTimestamp }>` | none | none | none |
34	| `resolveSession` | `(token: string) => Promise<SessionPrincipal \| null>` | none | none | none |
35	| `resolveActorForOrg` | `(principal: SessionPrincipal, orgSlug: string) => Promise<Actor \| null>` | none (builds the Actor) | none | none |
36	| `switchActiveOrg` | `(principal: SessionPrincipal, input: SwitchOrgInput) => Promise<void>` | none | none | plain `Error` (not a member) |
37	| `destroySession` | `(token: string) => Promise<void>` | none | none | none |
38	
39	## Collaborators
40	
41	- `src/server/repositories/user-repository.ts` — `findUserByEmail`, `insertUser`,
42	  `findPasswordHash`, `updatePasswordHash`, `findUserById`.
43	- `src/server/repositories/_password-reset-repository.ts` — `issueResetToken`,
44	  `findLiveResetToken`, `consumeResetToken`.
45	- `src/server/repositories/session-repository.ts` — `createSession`,
46	  `findSessionByTokenHash`, `revokeSession`, `purgeExpiredSessions`.
47	- `src/server/repositories/member-repository.ts` — `findMember`, `touchLastSeen`.
48	- `src/server/repositories/organization-repository.ts` — `findOrgBySlug`,
49	  `listOrgsForUser`.
50	- `src/lib/hash.ts` — `hashPassword`, `verifyPassword`, `hashToken`, `randomToken`.
51	- `src/lib/rate-limit.ts` — `consumeRateLimit`.
52	- `src/lib/slug.ts` — `slugify`, used by `register` to derive the seeded org's slug.
53	- `src/server/services/organization-service.ts` — `createOrganization`, called directly by
54	  `register`.
55	- `src/server/services/email-service.ts` — `renderEmail`, `sendEmail`.
56	- `src/lib/tenant.ts` — `assertOrgScope`, called by `session-service.ts` only.
57	
58	### DES-164 — auth-service declares it must call emit but cannot, because TaskflowEventMap has no authentication events
59	
60	- **Satisfies:** REQ-200, REQ-209
61	- **Decided in:** ADR-005
62	- **Code:** `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` (module-level doc comment)
63	
64	This is the one honest, explicit gap this design set is required to surface, and it is stated
65	in the source itself rather than inferred: the module doc comment reads "Must call (do not
66	reimplement): hashPassword, verifyPassword, consumeRateLimit, emit," immediately followed by a
67	second comment block: "`TaskflowEventMap` has no authentication event and the type is part of
68	the frozen contract, so the declared `emit` is not reachable from here." Reading the function
69	bodies confirms this literally — there is no `import { emit } from "@/lib/event-bus"` anywhere
70	in `auth-service.ts`, and no call to `emit` appears in `register`, `login`, `logout`,
71	`requestPasswordReset`, or `confirmPasswordReset`. The practical consequence: login attempts,
72	successful or failed, password resets, and logouts are entirely invisible to the event bus and
73	therefore to every listener built on top of it — `activity-service.ts`'s audit trail (DES-172
74	in `service-activity-and-attachment.md`) has no way to record "user X logged in" or "user X
75	reset their password" as an activity row, because there is no event to subscribe to for either.
76	The one authentication-adjacent action that *is* observable is registration's downstream
77	effect: `register` calls `createOrganization`, which does emit `member.joined` for the new
78	owner (DES-150 in `service-organization.md`) — so account creation is visible to the audit
79	trail only as a side effect of the organization it creates, never as an authentication event in
80	its own right. Anyone extending Taskflow's event map to add authentication events would need
81	an ADR, since the brief and the source comment both treat `TaskflowEventMap`'s closed 21-key
82	union as a frozen contract this service cannot unilaterally widen.
83	
84	### DES-165 — Login charges the rate-limit bucket before checking the password, so both failure modes are throttled identically
85	
86	- **Satisfies:** REQ-200, REQ-208
87	- **Decided in:** ADR-011
88	- **Code:** `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` — `login`, `LOGIN_BUCKET`,
89	  `ANONYMOUS_ORG`
90	
91	`login` calls `consumeRateLimit(ANONYMOUS_ORG, LOGIN_BUCKET)` as its very first line, before
92	`userRepo.findUserByEmail` is even called — `ANONYMOUS_ORG` is a fixed sentinel org id (a
93	27-zero string cast to `OrgId`), used specifically because, per the source comment, "rate
94	limiting before a session exists has no tenant to charge against, so every unauthenticated
95	attempt is billed to this sentinel bucket." This means every login attempt against Taskflow,
96	regardless of which organization the email eventually resolves to, shares one global rate
97	limit bucket rather than a per-org one — a deliberate departure from every other rate-limited
98	action in the service layer (comment creation, search, invites), all of which key on the real
99	`orgId`. `LOGIN_BUCKET` (`"auth:login"`) is not among the buckets the brief's product facts
100	enumerate explicitly by name alongside their capacity/refill numbers — only `auth:password
101	-reset` (5 capacity / 1 refill per minute) is named — so `auth:login` falls back to the
102	default bucket configuration (30 capacity / 10 refill per minute) documented in
103	`src/lib/rate-limit.ts`. Once the token is consumed, `login` proceeds to look up the user and
104	verify the password, and both the "no such user" and "wrong password" cases throw the
105	identical message "Those credentials did not match" — an enumeration-resistance choice that
106	extends the anti-enumeration reasoning DES-167 documents for password reset to the login path
107	as well, since a distinguishable "no such user" error would let an attacker enumerate
108	registered emails one login attempt at a time.
109	
110	### DES-166 — Registration is one call that creates a user, a workspace, and its owner membership, with no intermediate state
111	
112	- **Satisfies:** REQ-209
113	- **Decided in:** ADR-006
114	- **Code:** `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` — `register`
115	
116	`register` first checks `userRepo.findUserByEmail` and throws if an account already exists —
117	this is a plain uniqueness check, not itself an enumeration protection, since registration
118	necessarily reveals whether an email is taken (unlike login or reset, which do not need to).
119	It then inserts the user row with a hashed password, and immediately calls
120	`createOrganization(user.id, { name: \`${input.name}'s workspace\`, slug: slugify(input.name)
121	|| "workspace", plan: "free" })` — a synthesized workspace name and slug the user never
122	explicitly chose, always on the `free` plan regardless of anything in `RegisterInput`. The
123	`slugify(input.name) || "workspace"` fallback covers the case where a user's display name
124	contains no slug-safe characters at all (an all-emoji or all-symbol name, say), falling back
125	to the literal string `"workspace"` rather than producing an empty or invalid slug —
126	`organization-service.ts`'s own `uniqueSlug` call inside `createOrganization` then handles any
127	collision against existing org slugs. `register`'s final step renders and "sends" a `welcome`
128	template email via `email-service.ts`; per DES-132 in `service-digest-and-email.md`, this is a
129	structured log write, not a real delivery, but it happens synchronously as part of the
130	registration call, so a slow or failing render would delay the response the caller sees — the
131	function does not fire-and-forget this step.
132	
133	### DES-167 — Password reset resolves identically whether or not the email is known, and stores only the token's hash
134	
135	- **Satisfies:** REQ-200, REQ-201, REQ-208
136	- **Decided in:** ADR-020
137	- **Code:** `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` — `requestPasswordReset`,
138	  `confirmPasswordReset`, `RESET_TTL_MS`
139	
140	`requestPasswordReset` consumes the `auth:password-reset` bucket (5/1, the one named bucket in
141	the brief's rate-limit table) and then, if `!verdict.allowed`, simply `return`s — no thrown
142	error, no distinguishable response between a throttled request and one that proceeds. If the
143	user is not found, the function also just `return`s, with the same void result as a successful
144	send. The source comment states the reasoning directly: "telling an anonymous caller which
145	emails have accounts is an enumeration oracle." Because both branches produce an identical
146	`Promise<void>` with no observable difference to the caller, a script probing this endpoint
147	cannot distinguish "no such account," "rate limited," and "reset email sent" from the response
148	alone — REQ-208's rate limiting is real, but it is deliberately invisible to the caller for
149	this specific endpoint, unlike `login`'s rate limit, which does throw a visible message
150	(DES-165). The reset token itself is generated with `randomToken(32)`, and only `hashToken
151	(token)` is passed to `resetTokenRepo.issueResetToken` — the raw token exists solely inside
152	the rendered email, matching the same hash-only-at-rest discipline `session-service.ts`
153	applies to session tokens (DES-168) and REQ-201's "passwords are stored only as hashes"
154	extends by the same logic to reset tokens even though REQ-201 itself is about passwords, not
155	reset tokens specifically. `RESET_TTL_MS` is one hour (`60 * 60 * 1000`).
156	`confirmPasswordReset` marks the token consumed via `resetTokenRepo.consumeResetToken` *before*
157	writing the new password hash — the source comment: "a replay of the same link cannot
158	overwrite a password the user has since changed again" — so a delayed second submission of the
159	same reset link, arriving after a first successful reset, fails at the consumed-token check
160	rather than silently reverting the password a second time.
161	
162	### DES-168 — Session tokens are hashed at rest, and resolveSession never distinguishes an expired session from a nonexistent one
163	
164	- **Satisfies:** REQ-202, REQ-203, REQ-204
165	- **Decided in:** ADR-020
166	- **Code:** `src/server/services/session-service.ts` — `createSessionToken`,
167	  `resolveSession`, `SESSION_TTL_DAYS`
168	
169	`createSessionToken` generates a raw token via `randomToken(TOKEN_BYTES)` (32 bytes) and
170	stores only `hashToken(token)` via `sessionRepo.createSession` — the source comment: "only the
171	hash reaches the database, so a dump of the `sessions` table cannot be replayed as a login,"
172	mirroring the exact same pattern DES-167 documents for reset tokens. `SESSION_TTL_DAYS` is
173	`30`, matching the value the brief's product facts state and computed here as
174	`SESSION_TTL_DAYS * MS_PER_DAY` added to the current time for `expiresAt`. `resolveSession`
175	is a one-line passthrough to `sessionRepo.findSessionByTokenHash(hashToken(token))` — it
176	returns whatever the repository returns, `SessionPrincipal | null`, with no service-level logic
177	distinguishing "token never existed" from "token existed but its row has since expired or been
178	purged"; whether an expired-but-not-yet-purged row is still returned as a live principal is
179	entirely a property of `session-repository.ts`'s own query, not something this service layers
180	on top of. `resolveSession` performs no authorization of its own — it is the raw lookup
181	primitive `resolveActorForOrg` builds on.
182	
183	### DES-169 — resolveActorForOrg re-asserts scope on an Actor it just built from the same org, and this redundancy is intentional
184	
185	- **Satisfies:** REQ-210, REQ-211, REQ-212, REQ-213
186	- **Decided in:** ADR-013, ADR-007
187	- **Code:** `src/server/services/session-service.ts` — `resolveActorForOrg`,
188	  `switchActiveOrg`
189	
190	`resolveActorForOrg(principal, orgSlug)` resolves the org by slug, loads the caller's
191	membership row in that specific org, returns `null` unless a row exists and `status ===
192	"active"` (the same active-only rule `member-service.ts`'s `resolveActor` applies, DES-145 in
193	`service-member-and-invitation.md` — the two functions duplicate this check rather than
194	sharing a helper), constructs the `Actor` inline, and then calls `assertOrgScope(actor, org
195	.id)` on an `Actor` it just built to reference that exact org id. The source comment
196	acknowledges the apparent redundancy directly: "the `assertOrgScope` call at the end looks
197	redundant — the actor was just built from that org — but it is the invariant this whole layer
198	exists to uphold, and it catches a mis-wired membership lookup immediately." In other words,
199	the assertion is not there to catch a malicious caller (there is none reachable at this layer)
200	but to catch a *bug* in this very function — if a future edit changed which `orgId` field
201	feeds the `Actor` construction, this assertion would fail loudly in development rather than
202	silently minting a cross-tenant `Actor`. Once the actor passes, `resolveActorForOrg` calls
203	`memberRepo.touchLastSeen`, updating presence as a side effect of every org-scoped page load,
204	not as a separate tracked action. `switchActiveOrg` performs a near-identical membership
205	re-check (REQ-009's explicit-switch requirement) but, notably, does not itself write the
206	session's active-org column — the source comment explains `SessionPrincipal` carries no
207	session id, so `sessionRepository.setActiveOrg` is called by the Server Action that still
208	holds the cookie, with this function owning only the authorization half of the switch.
209	`destroySession` similarly cannot target a specific session row directly for the same
210	structural reason (`SessionPrincipal` has no session id): it resolves the principal from the
211	token, then calls `sessionRepo.purgeExpiredSessions`, a sweep rather than a targeted delete —
212	REQ-207's "logout destroys the session server-side" is satisfied by this sweep clearing the
213	now-expired-or-flagged row rather than by an id-targeted deletion, a detail worth flagging
214	since it means logout's server-side cleanup is coupled to whatever `purgeExpiredSessions`
215	considers eligible for removal, not to the specific token that was presented.
216	
217	## Sequence: login through to a resolved per-organization Actor
218	
219	```mermaid
220	sequenceDiagram
221	    participant UI as Login form
222	    participant Auth as auth-service.login
223	    participant RateLimit as rate-limit.consumeRateLimit
224	    participant UserRepo as user-repository
225	    participant Session as session-service.createSessionToken
226	    participant SessionRepo as session-repository
227	    participant Proxy as src/proxy.ts
228	    participant ResolveOrg as session-service.resolveActorForOrg
229	
230	    UI->>Auth: login({email, password})
231	    Auth->>RateLimit: consumeRateLimit(ANONYMOUS_ORG, "auth:login")
232	    RateLimit-->>Auth: allowed
233	    Auth->>UserRepo: findUserByEmail
234	    UserRepo-->>Auth: user
235	    Auth->>UserRepo: findPasswordHash
236	    Auth->>Auth: verifyPassword(password, hash)
237	    Auth->>Session: createSessionToken(user.id)
238	    Session->>SessionRepo: createSession(userId, hashToken(token), expiresAt)
239	    Session-->>Auth: {token, expiresAt}
240	    Auth-->>UI: {user, token}
241	    Note over UI,Proxy: cookie set by the caller, not this service
242	    UI->>Proxy: subsequent request with session cookie
243	    Proxy->>ResolveOrg: resolveActorForOrg(principal, orgSlug)
244	    ResolveOrg->>ResolveOrg: findOrgBySlug + findMember + assertOrgScope
245	    ResolveOrg-->>Proxy: Actor
246	```
247	
248	1. The login form submits credentials; the rate-limit bucket is consumed before the user
249	   lookup, so a brute-force script is throttled on every attempt, successful or not.
250	2. `verifyPassword` compares against the stored hash; a failure and a nonexistent user both
251	   produce the identical thrown message.
252	3. On success, `login` calls `session-service.ts`'s `createSessionToken`, which generates the
253	   raw token, hashes it for storage, and returns the raw token to the caller — the only place
254	   the raw value exists is this return value and whatever the caller does with it next.
255	4. `login` itself never touches a cookie; per REQ-206, only `src/lib/session.ts` is trusted to
256	   read or write it, so the Server Action that called `login` is responsible for setting it.
257	5. On a later request, `src/proxy.ts` (REQ-212's request hook, ADR-007) reads the cookie,
258	   resolves the principal, and calls `resolveActorForOrg` with the org slug from the URL.
259	6. `resolveActorForOrg` re-derives membership from scratch for that specific org and asserts
260	   scope on the `Actor` it just built, per DES-169, before any downstream service call can
261	   treat it as authorized.
262	
263	## Failure modes
264	
265	| thrown error | resulting error code | caller behaviour |
266	|---|---|---|
267	| plain `Error` (email taken in `register`) | falls through to `internal_error` (500) | signup form shows a generic "could not create account" message keyed off the thrown text |
268	| plain `Error` (rate limit / bad credentials in `login`) | falls through to `internal_error` (500) | login form shows one generic error for both cases, matching the enumeration-resistance intent even though the HTTP status itself does not distinguish rate limiting from bad credentials |
269	| plain `Error` (rate limit / invalid token in `confirmPasswordReset`) | falls through to `internal_error` (500) | reset form shows "that reset link is no longer valid" or a generic retry message |
270	| no throw at all (`requestPasswordReset` on unknown email or throttled request) | n/a — resolves successfully | UI always shows "if that email has an account, a reset link was sent," regardless of what actually happened server-side |
271	| `switchActiveOrg`'s plain `Error` (not a member) | falls through to `internal_error` (500) | org switcher only lists orgs the user already belongs to, so this mainly guards a stale client-side list |
272	
273	All of the auth path's thrown errors are plain `Error` instances, none of the typed domain
274	error classes (`PermissionDeniedError`, `TenantScopeError`, and so on) — consistent with there
275	being no `Actor` yet for most of these calls to check permissions against in the first place,
276	so the untyped-error pattern flagged elsewhere in this design set (`service-issue.md` DES-101,
277	`service-billing-and-usage.md` DES-137) is, for this specific service, less an inconsistency
278	than a reflection of auth genuinely having no `PermissionResource` to build.
279	
280	## Test coverage
281	
282	`tests/schemas/auth.schema.test.ts` covers the Zod schemas (`RegisterInput`, `LoginInput`,
283	`PasswordResetRequestInput`, `PasswordResetConfirmInput`) these functions accept, not the
284	service functions' own logic. There is no dedicated tests/services/auth-service.test.ts or
285	tests/services/session-service.test.ts in the corpus's test directory — the rate-limit
286	ordering in DES-165, the enumeration-resistant behaviour in DES-167, the token-hashing
287	discipline in DES-168, and the redundant-but-intentional scope assertion in DES-169 are all
288	currently verifiable only by reading `auth-service.ts` and `session-service.ts` directly, not
289	by pointing at a passing automated test — a real gap worth flagging given how much of this
290	design set's discussion concerns security-sensitive behaviour (rate limiting, token hashing,
291	enumeration resistance) that has no dedicated regression coverage.

- **Satisfies:** REQ-200, REQ-209
- **Decided in:** ADR-005
- **Code:** `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` (module-level doc comment)

This is the one honest, explicit gap this design set is required to surface, and it is stated
in the source itself rather than inferred: the module doc comment reads "Must call (do not
reimplement): hashPassword, verifyPassword, consumeRateLimit, emit," immediately followed by a
second comment block: "`TaskflowEventMap` has no authentication event and the type is part of
the frozen contract, so the declared `emit` is not reachable from here." Reading the function
bodies confirms this literally — there is no `import { emit } from "@/lib/event-bus"` anywhere
in `auth-service.ts`, and no call to `emit` appears in `register`, `login`, `logout`,
`requestPasswordReset`, or `confirmPasswordReset`. The practical consequence: login attempts,
successful or failed, password resets, and logouts are entirely invisible to the event bus and
therefore to every listener built on top of it — `activity-service.ts`'s audit trail (DES-172
in `service-activity-and-attachment.md`) has no way to record "user X logged in" or "user X
reset their password" as an activity row, because there is no event to subscribe to for either.
The one authentication-adjacent action that *is* observable is registration's downstream
effect: `register` calls `createOrganization`, which does emit `member.joined` for the new
owner (DES-150 in `service-organization.md`) — so account creation is visible to the audit
trail only as a side effect of the organization it creates, never as an authentication event in
its own right. Anyone extending Taskflow's event map to add authentication events would need
an ADR, since the brief and the source comment both treat `TaskflowEventMap`'s closed 21-key
union as a frozen contract this service cannot unilaterally widen.

### DES-165 — Login charges the rate-limit bucket before checking the password, so both failure modes are throttled identically

- **Satisfies:** REQ-200, REQ-208
- **Decided in:** ADR-011
- **Code:** `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` — `login`, `LOGIN_BUCKET`,
  `ANONYMOUS_ORG`

`login` calls `consumeRateLimit(ANONYMOUS_ORG, LOGIN_BUCKET)` as its very first line, before
`userRepo.findUserByEmail` is even called — `ANONYMOUS_ORG` is a fixed sentinel org id (a
27-zero string cast to `OrgId`), used specifically because, per the source comment, "rate
limiting before a session exists has no tenant to charge against, so every unauthenticated
attempt is billed to this sentinel bucket." This means every login attempt against Taskflow,
regardless of which organization the email eventually resolves to, shares one global rate
limit bucket rather than a per-org one — a deliberate departure from every other rate-limited
action in the service layer (comment creation, search, invites), all of which key on the real
`orgId`. `LOGIN_BUCKET` (`"auth:login"`) is not among the buckets the brief's product facts
enumerate explicitly by name alongside their capacity/refill numbers — only `auth:password
-reset` (5 capacity / 1 refill per minute) is named — so `auth:login` falls back to the
default bucket configuration (30 capacity / 10 refill per minute) documented in
`src/lib/rate-limit.ts`. Once the token is consumed, `login` proceeds to look up the user and
verify the password, and both the "no such user" and "wrong password" cases throw the
identical message "Those credentials did not match" — an enumeration-resistance choice that
extends the anti-enumeration reasoning DES-167 documents for password reset to the login path
as well, since a distinguishable "no such user" error would let an attacker enumerate
registered emails one login attempt at a time.

### DES-166 — Registration is one call that creates a user, a workspace, and its owner membership, with no intermediate state

- **Satisfies:** REQ-209
- **Decided in:** ADR-006
- **Code:** `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` — `register`

`register` first checks `userRepo.findUserByEmail` and throws if an account already exists —
this is a plain uniqueness check, not itself an enumeration protection, since registration
necessarily reveals whether an email is taken (unlike login or reset, which do not need to).
It then inserts the user row with a hashed password, and immediately calls
`createOrganization(user.id, { name: \`${input.name}'s workspace\`, slug: slugify(input.name)
|| "workspace", plan: "free" })` — a synthesized workspace name and slug the user never
explicitly chose, always on the `free` plan regardless of anything in `RegisterInput`. The
`slugify(input.name) || "workspace"` fallback covers the case where a user's display name
contains no slug-safe characters at all (an all-emoji or all-symbol name, say), falling back
to the literal string `"workspace"` rather than producing an empty or invalid slug —
`organization-service.ts`'s own `uniqueSlug` call inside `createOrganization` then handles any
collision against existing org slugs. `register`'s final step renders and "sends" a `welcome`
template email via `email-service.ts`; per DES-132 in `service-digest-and-email.md`, this is a
structured log write, not a real delivery, but it happens synchronously as part of the
registration call, so a slow or failing render would delay the response the caller sees — the
function does not fire-and-forget this step.

### DES-167 — Password reset resolves identically whether or not the email is known, and stores only the token's hash

- **Satisfies:** REQ-200, REQ-201, REQ-208
- **Decided in:** ADR-020
- **Code:** `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` — `requestPasswordReset`,
  `confirmPasswordReset`, `RESET_TTL_MS`

`requestPasswordReset` consumes the `auth:password-reset` bucket (5/1, the one named bucket in
the brief's rate-limit table) and then, if `!verdict.allowed`, simply `return`s — no thrown
error, no distinguishable response between a throttled request and one that proceeds. If the
user is not found, the function also just `return`s, with the same void result as a successful
send. The source comment states the reasoning directly: "telling an anonymous caller which
emails have accounts is an enumeration oracle." Because both branches produce an identical
`Promise<void>` with no observable difference to the caller, a script probing this endpoint
cannot distinguish "no such account," "rate limited," and "reset email sent" from the response
alone — REQ-208's rate limiting is real, but it is deliberately invisible to the caller for
this specific endpoint, unlike `login`'s rate limit, which does throw a visible message
(DES-165). The reset token itself is generated with `randomToken(32)`, and only `hashToken
(token)` is passed to `resetTokenRepo.issueResetToken` — the raw token exists solely inside
the rendered email, matching the same hash-only-at-rest discipline `session-service.ts`
applies to session tokens (DES-168) and REQ-201's "passwords are stored only as hashes"
extends by the same logic to reset tokens even though REQ-201 itself is about passwords, not
reset tokens specifically. `RESET_TTL_MS` is one hour (`60 * 60 * 1000`).
`confirmPasswordReset` marks the token consumed via `resetTokenRepo.consumeResetToken` *before*
writing the new password hash — the source comment: "a replay of the same link cannot
overwrite a password the user has since changed again" — so a delayed second submission of the
same reset link, arriving after a first successful reset, fails at the consumed-token check
rather than silently reverting the password a second time.

### DES-168 — Session tokens are hashed at rest, and resolveSession never distinguishes an expired session from a nonexistent one

- **Satisfies:** REQ-202, REQ-203, REQ-204
- **Decided in:** ADR-020
- **Code:** `src/server/services/session-service.ts` — `createSessionToken`,
  `resolveSession`, `SESSION_TTL_DAYS`

`createSessionToken` generates a raw token via `randomToken(TOKEN_BYTES)` (32 bytes) and
stores only `hashToken(token)` via `sessionRepo.createSession` — the source comment: "only the
hash reaches the database, so a dump of the `sessions` table cannot be replayed as a login,"
mirroring the exact same pattern DES-167 documents for reset tokens. `SESSION_TTL_DAYS` is
`30`, matching the value the brief's product facts state and computed here as
`SESSION_TTL_DAYS * MS_PER_DAY` added to the current time for `expiresAt`. `resolveSession`
is a one-line passthrough to `sessionRepo.findSessionByTokenHash(hashToken(token))` — it
returns whatever the repository returns, `SessionPrincipal | null`, with no service-level logic
distinguishing "token never existed" from "token existed but its row has since expired or been
purged"; whether an expired-but-not-yet-purged row is still returned as a live principal is
entirely a property of `session-repository.ts`'s own query, not something this service layers
on top of. `resolveSession` performs no authorization of its own — it is the raw lookup
primitive `resolveActorForOrg` builds on.

### DES-169 — resolveActorForOrg re-asserts scope on an Actor it just built from the same org, and this redundancy is intentional

- **Satisfies:** REQ-210, REQ-211, REQ-212, REQ-213
- **Decided in:** ADR-013, ADR-007
- **Code:** `src/server/services/session-service.ts` — `resolveActorForOrg`,
  `switchActiveOrg`

`resolveActorForOrg(principal, orgSlug)` resolves the org by slug, loads the caller's
membership row in that specific org, returns `null` unless a row exists and `status ===
"active"` (the same active-only rule `member-service.ts`'s `resolveActor` applies, DES-145 in
`service-member-and-invitation.md` — the two functions duplicate this check rather than
sharing a helper), constructs the `Actor` inline, and then calls `assertOrgScope(actor, org
.id)` on an `Actor` it just built to reference that exact org id. The source comment
acknowledges the apparent redundancy directly: "the `assertOrgScope` call at the end looks
redundant — the actor was just built from that org — but it is the invariant this whole layer
exists to uphold, and it catches a mis-wired membership lookup immediately." In other words,
the assertion is not there to catch a malicious caller (there is none reachable at this layer)
but to catch a *bug* in this very function — if a future edit changed which `orgId` field
feeds the `Actor` construction, this assertion would fail loudly in development rather than
silently minting a cross-tenant `Actor`. Once the actor passes, `resolveActorForOrg` calls
`memberRepo.touchLastSeen`, updating presence as a side effect of every org-scoped page load,
not as a separate tracked action. `switchActiveOrg` performs a near-identical membership
re-check (REQ-009's explicit-switch requirement) but, notably, does not itself write the
session's active-org column — the source comment explains `SessionPrincipal` carries no
session id, so `sessionRepository.setActiveOrg` is called by the Server Action that still
holds the cookie, with this function owning only the authorization half of the switch.
`destroySession` similarly cannot target a specific session row directly for the same
structural reason (`SessionPrincipal` has no session id): it resolves the principal from the
token, then calls `sessionRepo.purgeExpiredSessions`, a sweep rather than a targeted delete —
REQ-207's "logout destroys the session server-side" is satisfied by this sweep clearing the
now-expired-or-flagged row rather than by an id-targeted deletion, a detail worth flagging
since it means logout's server-side cleanup is coupled to whatever `purgeExpiredSessions`
considers eligible for removal, not to the specific token that was presented.

## Sequence: login through to a resolved per-organization Actor

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant UI as Login form
    participant Auth as auth-service.login
    participant RateLimit as rate-limit.consumeRateLimit
    participant UserRepo as user-repository
    participant Session as session-service.createSessionToken
    participant SessionRepo as session-repository
    participant Proxy as src/proxy.ts
    participant ResolveOrg as session-service.resolveActorForOrg

    UI->>Auth: login({email, password})
    Auth->>RateLimit: consumeRateLimit(ANONYMOUS_ORG, "auth:login")
    RateLimit-->>Auth: allowed
    Auth->>UserRepo: findUserByEmail
    UserRepo-->>Auth: user
    Auth->>UserRepo: findPasswordHash
    Auth->>Auth: verifyPassword(password, hash)
    Auth->>Session: createSessionToken(user.id)
    Session->>SessionRepo: createSession(userId, hashToken(token), expiresAt)
    Session-->>Auth: {token, expiresAt}
    Auth-->>UI: {user, token}
    Note over UI,Proxy: cookie set by the caller, not this service
    UI->>Proxy: subsequent request with session cookie
    Proxy->>ResolveOrg: resolveActorForOrg(principal, orgSlug)
    ResolveOrg->>ResolveOrg: findOrgBySlug + findMember + assertOrgScope
    ResolveOrg-->>Proxy: Actor
```

1. The login form submits credentials; the rate-limit bucket is consumed before the user
   lookup, so a brute-force script is throttled on every attempt, successful or not.
2. `verifyPassword` compares against the stored hash; a failure and a nonexistent user both
   produce the identical thrown message.
3. On success, `login` calls `session-service.ts`'s `createSessionToken`, which generates the
   raw token, hashes it for storage, and returns the raw token to the caller — the only place
   the raw value exists is this return value and whatever the caller does with it next.
4. `login` itself never touches a cookie; per REQ-206, only `src/lib/session.ts` is trusted to
   read or write it, so the Server Action that called `login` is responsible for setting it.
5. On a later request, `src/proxy.ts` (REQ-212's request hook, ADR-007) reads the cookie,
   resolves the principal, and calls `resolveActorForOrg` with the org slug from the URL.
6. `resolveActorForOrg` re-derives membership from scratch for that specific org and asserts
   scope on the `Actor` it just built, per DES-169, before any downstream service call can
   treat it as authorized.

## Failure modes

| thrown error | resulting error code | caller behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| plain `Error` (email taken in `register`) | falls through to `internal_error` (500) | signup form shows a generic "could not create account" message keyed off the thrown text |
| plain `Error` (rate limit / bad credentials in `login`) | falls through to `internal_error` (500) | login form shows one generic error for both cases, matching the enumeration-resistance intent even though the HTTP status itself does not distinguish rate limiting from bad credentials |
| plain `Error` (rate limit / invalid token in `confirmPasswordReset`) | falls through to `internal_error` (500) | reset form shows "that reset link is no longer valid" or a generic retry message |
| no throw at all (`requestPasswordReset` on unknown email or throttled request) | n/a — resolves successfully | UI always shows "if that email has an account, a reset link was sent," regardless of what actually happened server-side |
| `switchActiveOrg`'s plain `Error` (not a member) | falls through to `internal_error` (500) | org switcher only lists orgs the user already belongs to, so this mainly guards a stale client-side list |

All of the auth path's thrown errors are plain `Error` instances, none of the typed domain
error classes (`PermissionDeniedError`, `TenantScopeError`, and so on) — consistent with there
being no `Actor` yet for most of these calls to check permissions against in the first place,
so the untyped-error pattern flagged elsewhere in this design set (`service-issue.md` DES-101,
`service-billing-and-usage.md` DES-137) is, for this specific service, less an inconsistency
than a reflection of auth genuinely having no `PermissionResource` to build.

## Test coverage

`tests/schemas/auth.schema.test.ts` covers the Zod schemas (`RegisterInput`, `LoginInput`,
`PasswordResetRequestInput`, `PasswordResetConfirmInput`) these functions accept, not the
service functions' own logic. There is no dedicated tests/services/auth-service.test.ts or
tests/services/session-service.test.ts in the corpus's test directory — the rate-limit
ordering in DES-165, the enumeration-resistant behaviour in DES-167, the token-hashing
discipline in DES-168, and the redundant-but-intentional scope assertion in DES-169 are all
currently verifiable only by reading `auth-service.ts` and `session-service.ts` directly, not
by pointing at a passing automated test — a real gap worth flagging given how much of this
design set's discussion concerns security-sensitive behaviour (rate limiting, token hashing,
enumeration resistance) that has no dedicated regression coverage.

9	
10	## Scope
11	
12	This document defines the requirements for credential authentication, session lifecycle, the
13	request-hook gate, and how a request resolves into an organization-scoped `Actor`. It covers
14	login, registration, logout, password reset, session cookie handling, and multi-organization
15	membership from the session's point of view. It does not cover role or permission mechanics
16	once an `Actor` exists (`membership-and-roles.md`) or organization creation's business rules
17	beyond the registration flow that triggers it (`organizations.md`).
18	
19	## Context
20	
21	`auth-service.ts` owns credential login, registration and password reset; there is no
22	third-party identity provider anywhere in Taskflow — every account is email and password,
23	hashed with `node:crypto`'s scrypt through `src/lib/hash.ts`'s `hashPassword`/
24	`verifyPassword`, never stored or compared in plaintext. `register(input)` creates a `User`
25	and, in the same call, an `Organization` via `organization-service.ts#createOrganization`
26	(`REQ-003`), so registration and org creation are inseparable in Taskflow — there is no
27	"create an account first, decide on an organization later" path; a brand-new user always
28	lands with a first organization already provisioned.
29	
30	Sessions are opaque tokens (`ADR-020`), not JWTs: `createSessionToken(userId)` in
31	`session-service.ts` generates a random token, stores only its hash
32	(`session-repository.ts#createSession`, using `hashToken`), and returns the plaintext token
33	to the caller once, for the cookie. `resolveSession(token)` hashes the incoming cookie value
34	and looks up the hash, so a database compromise never exposes usable session tokens
35	directly — the same defensive pattern invitation tokens use (`REQ-029`). Sessions expire
36	after `SESSION_TTL_DAYS = 14`, defined in `session-service.ts` itself rather than in
37	`src/config/constants.ts`, since it is specifically a session concern, not a general
38	cross-cutting constant.
39	
40	`src/lib/session.ts` is the one module permitted to read or write the session cookie
41	(`REQ-206`); every other module that needs the session goes through
42	`getSessionPrincipal()`, which returns a `SessionPrincipal` — the pre-organization identity —
43	distinct from an `Actor`, which is always resolved for one specific organization
44	(`REQ-210`). `src/lib/actor.ts#getActor(orgSlug)` is the bridge: it calls
45	`getSessionPrincipal()`, then `resolveActorForOrg(principal, orgSlug)` in
46	`session-service.ts`, which itself calls `member-service.ts#resolveActor` to look up the
47	caller's membership and role in that specific organization. A `SessionPrincipal` with no
48	membership in the requested org yields `null` from `resolveActorForOrg`, and `getActor`
49	turns that into a thrown `unauthorized`/`forbidden` for the caller.
50	
51	The cookie itself is `httpOnly`, `sameSite: 'lax'`, and `secure` in production, named by
52	`SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` declared in `src/schemas/session.ts` — not `src/config/constants.ts`,
53	because the cookie name is validated as part of the session schema rather than treated as an
54	unrelated constant. In Next.js 16, `cookies()` is async, which is why every function in
55	`src/lib/session.ts` is async even where the underlying operation feels like it should be
56	synchronous — this is a framework fact worth stating plainly since it is easy to miss in a
57	quick read of the module and write a synchronous caller that then fails to compile.
58	
59	There is no `middleware.ts` in this codebase; the request-hook gate is `src/proxy.ts`,
60	exporting `proxy` (`ADR-007`, `REQ-212`), Next 16's renamed middleware concept — every
61	request to a dashboard route passes through it before any page component runs, and it is
62	where an unauthenticated request to a protected route is redirected to login (`REQ-211`).
63	
64	## Open questions
65	
66	1. `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` documents in its own comments that it must call
67	   `emit()` on login and registration but cannot, because `TaskflowEventMap` has no auth
68	   events — meaning login and registration currently produce no activity-feed row and no
69	   webhook-eligible event, an intentional gap noted in the brief rather than something this
70	   document can resolve.
71	2. `REQ-204`'s fixed 30-day session lifetime has no "remember me" variant or shorter-lived
72	   option; whether sensitive actions (billing changes, org deletion) should require a
73	   freshly re-verified session rather than relying on the same 30-day token is unspecified.
74	3. `REQ-213` establishes a user can belong to several organizations, but there is no
75	   requirement here describing what happens to a user's sessions when their last
76	   organization membership is removed — whether the session simply resolves no actor for
77	   any org slug thereafter, or is explicitly revoked.
78	
79	### REQ-200 — Users authenticate with email and password
80	
81	- **Priority:** must
82	- **Status:** implemented
83	- **Related:** REQ-201, REQ-209
84	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` — `login`, `src/server/repositories/user-repository.ts` — `findUserByEmail`
85	- **Verified by:** `tests/schemas/auth.schema.test.ts`
86	
87	There is no OAuth, SSO or magic-link path in Taskflow; `login(input)` in `auth-service.ts`
88	takes an email and password, looks up the user by email
89	(`user-repository.ts#findUserByEmail`), and verifies the password against the stored hash.
90	This is a deliberate scope limitation for a product aimed at small-to-mid teams that do not
91	require enterprise identity federation on day one.
92	
93	**Acceptance criteria**
94	
95	1. `loginSchema` requires both an email and a password field; there is no alternate
96	   credential type accepted.
97	2. A login attempt against a non-existent email fails with the same generic error a wrong
98	   password would, avoiding user enumeration through differing error messages.
99	3. `findUserByEmail` is case-normalized so `User@Example.com` and `user@example.com` resolve
100	   to the same account.
101	
102	### REQ-201 — Passwords are stored only as hashes
103	
104	- **Priority:** must
105	- **Status:** implemented
106	- **Related:** ADR-020, REQ-200
107	- **Implemented by:** `src/lib/hash.ts` — `hashPassword`, `verifyPassword`
108	- **Verified by:** `tests/lib/hash.test.ts`
109	
110	`hashPassword`/`verifyPassword` in `src/lib/hash.ts` use `node:crypto`'s scrypt, with no
111	external hashing dependency. `insertUser` never receives a plaintext password parameter — its
112	input type is `{ email: string; name: string; passwordHash: string }`, so a plaintext
113	password literally cannot reach the repository layer through the type system.
114	
115	**Acceptance criteria**
116	
117	1. No repository or schema type includes a plaintext `password` field alongside a stored
118	   user record; only `passwordHash`.
119	2. `verifyPassword` performs a comparison resistant to short-circuit timing differences (the
120	   underlying scrypt-based comparison, not a naive string equality check).
121	3. `hashPassword`'s output differs between two calls with the same input password, since a
122	   fresh salt is used each time.
123	
124	### REQ-202 — Login issues an opaque session token
125	
126	- **Priority:** must
127	- **Status:** implemented
128	- **Related:** REQ-203, ADR-020
129	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/services/session-service.ts` — `createSessionToken`, `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` — `login`
130	- **Verified by:** none — covered indirectly; see the gaps section of the test plan
131	
132	`login` calls `createSessionToken(user.id)` and returns both the `User` and the plaintext
133	`token` to the caller (`loginAction`), which is the only point in the whole flow where the
134	plaintext token exists outside the browser — `setSessionCookie` writes it into the cookie
135	immediately, and from then on only its hash is ever referenced.
136	
137	**Acceptance criteria**
138	
139	1. `login`'s returned token is a high-entropy random value, not derived from any
140	   user-guessable input like the user id or email.
141	2. The token is never logged in plaintext by `src/lib/logger.ts`'s structured logger.
142	3. A successful login always produces exactly one new session row, not zero and not more
143	   than one.
144	
145	### REQ-203 — Session tokens are stored hashed
146	
147	- **Priority:** must
148	- **Status:** implemented
149	- **Related:** REQ-029, ADR-020
150	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/repositories/session-repository.ts` — `createSession`, `findSessionByTokenHash`, `src/lib/hash.ts` — `hashToken`
151	- **Verified by:** `tests/lib/hash.test.ts`
152	
153	`createSession(userId, tokenHash, expiresAt)` in `session-repository.ts` never receives a
154	plaintext token; `hashToken` in `src/lib/hash.ts` is applied before the value reaches the
155	repository, mirroring the invitation-token pattern (`REQ-029`) exactly, since both are
156	"a database leak should not hand out usable bearer credentials" problems solved the same
157	way.
158	
159	**Acceptance criteria**
160	
161	1. `findSessionByTokenHash` is the only lookup function; there is no lookup by plaintext
162	   token anywhere in the repository.
163	2. A leaked database backup does not, by itself, contain any value usable to authenticate as
164	   an existing session.
165	3. `hashToken` is deterministic for a given input, so the same plaintext token always
166	   resolves to the same session row on subsequent requests within its lifetime.
167	
168	### REQ-204 — Sessions expire after a fixed lifetime
169	
170	- **Priority:** must
171	- **Status:** implemented
172	- **Related:** REQ-207, ADR-020
173	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/services/session-service.ts` — `createSessionToken`, `resolveSession`, `src/server/repositories/session-repository.ts` — `purgeExpiredSessions`
174	- **Verified by:** none — covered indirectly; see the gaps section of the test plan
175	
176	`SESSION_TTL_DAYS = 30` in `session-service.ts`. `createSessionToken` computes `expiresAt`
177	from this constant at creation time; there is no sliding-window renewal that extends a
178	session's life on activity — a session created today expires in exactly 30 days regardless
179	of how often it is used in between.
180	
181	**Acceptance criteria**
182	
183	1. `resolveSession` returns `null` for a token whose stored `expiresAt` has passed, even if
184	   the session row has not yet been purged.
185	2. `purgeExpiredSessions(now)` in `session-repository.ts` removes expired rows in bulk,
186	   called from a cleanup path rather than on every request.
187	3. `SESSION_TTL_DAYS` is a single named constant, not a value duplicated at both the
188	   creation site and the expiry-check site.
189	
190	### REQ-205 — The session cookie is httpOnly and same-site lax
191	
192	- **Priority:** must
193	- **Status:** implemented
194	- **Related:** REQ-206, ADR-020
195	- **Implemented by:** `src/lib/session.ts` — `setSessionCookie`, `src/config/env.ts` — `env`
196	- **Verified by:** none — covered indirectly; see the gaps section of the test plan
197	
198	`setSessionCookie` sets `httpOnly: true` (unreadable from client-side JavaScript, mitigating
199	XSS-based token theft), `sameSite: 'lax'` (sent on top-level navigation but not on
200	cross-site subresource requests, mitigating CSRF while still allowing a user to click a
201	link from an email into the app and remain logged in), and `secure: true` only in
202	production, since local development over plain HTTP would otherwise refuse to set the
203	cookie at all.
204	
205	**Acceptance criteria**
206	
207	1. The cookie is never set with `httpOnly: false`.
208	2. `sameSite` is `'lax'`, not `'none'` or `'strict'` — `'strict'` would break the
209	   click-through-from-email login case the product relies on for invitation and

---
title: Authentication and sessions requirements
id: REQ-AUTH
status: approved
owners: [product-team, d.okafor]
last_updated: 2026-06-09
related: [REQ-001, REQ-003, ADR-020, DES-210]
---

## Scope

This document defines the requirements for credential authentication, session lifecycle, the
request-hook gate, and how a request resolves into an organization-scoped `Actor`. It covers
login, registration, logout, password reset, session cookie handling, and multi-organization
membership from the session's point of view. It does not cover role or permission mechanics
once an `Actor` exists (`membership-and-roles.md`) or organization creation's business rules
beyond the registration flow that triggers it (`organizations.md`).

## Context

`auth-service.ts` owns credential login, registration and password reset; there is no
third-party identity provider anywhere in Taskflow — every account is email and password,
hashed with `node:crypto`'s scrypt through `src/lib/hash.ts`'s `hashPassword`/
`verifyPassword`, never stored or compared in plaintext. `register(input)` creates a `User`
and, in the same call, an `Organization` via `organization-service.ts#createOrganization`
(`REQ-003`), so registration and org creation are inseparable in Taskflow — there is no
"create an account first, decide on an organization later" path; a brand-new user always
lands with a first organization already provisioned.

Sessions are opaque tokens (`ADR-020`), not JWTs: `createSessionToken(userId)` in
`session-service.ts` generates a random token, stores only its hash
(`session-repository.ts#createSession`, using `hashToken`), and returns the plaintext token
to the caller once, for the cookie. `resolveSession(token)` hashes the incoming cookie value
and looks up the hash, so a database compromise never exposes usable session tokens
directly — the same defensive pattern invitation tokens use (`REQ-029`). Sessions expire
after `SESSION_TTL_DAYS = 14`, defined in `session-service.ts` itself rather than in
`src/config/constants.ts`, since it is specifically a session concern, not a general
cross-cutting constant.

`src/lib/session.ts` is the one module permitted to read or write the session cookie
(`REQ-206`); every other module that needs the session goes through
`getSessionPrincipal()`, which returns a `SessionPrincipal` — the pre-organization identity —
distinct from an `Actor`, which is always resolved for one specific organization
(`REQ-210`). `src/lib/actor.ts#getActor(orgSlug)` is the bridge: it calls
`getSessionPrincipal()`, then `resolveActorForOrg(principal, orgSlug)` in
`session-service.ts`, which itself calls `member-service.ts#resolveActor` to look up the
caller's membership and role in that specific organization. A `SessionPrincipal` with no
membership in the requested org yields `null` from `resolveActorForOrg`, and `getActor`
turns that into a thrown `unauthorized`/`forbidden` for the caller.

The cookie itself is `httpOnly`, `sameSite: 'lax'`, and `secure` in production, named by
`SESSION_COOKIE_NAME` declared in `src/schemas/session.ts` — not `src/config/constants.ts`,
because the cookie name is validated as part of the session schema rather than treated as an
unrelated constant. In Next.js 16, `cookies()` is async, which is why every function in
`src/lib/session.ts` is async even where the underlying operation feels like it should be
synchronous — this is a framework fact worth stating plainly since it is easy to miss in a
quick read of the module and write a synchronous caller that then fails to compile.

There is no `middleware.ts` in this codebase; the request-hook gate is `src/proxy.ts`,
exporting `proxy` (`ADR-007`, `REQ-212`), Next 16's renamed middleware concept — every
request to a dashboard route passes through it before any page component runs, and it is
where an unauthenticated request to a protected route is redirected to login (`REQ-211`).

## Open questions

1. `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` documents in its own comments that it must call
   `emit()` on login and registration but cannot, because `TaskflowEventMap` has no auth
   events — meaning login and registration currently produce no activity-feed row and no
   webhook-eligible event, an intentional gap noted in the brief rather than something this
   document can resolve.
2. `REQ-204`'s fixed 30-day session lifetime has no "remember me" variant or shorter-lived
   option; whether sensitive actions (billing changes, org deletion) should require a
   freshly re-verified session rather than relying on the same 30-day token is unspecified.
3. `REQ-213` establishes a user can belong to several organizations, but there is no
   requirement here describing what happens to a user's sessions when their last
   organization membership is removed — whether the session simply resolves no actor for
   any org slug thereafter, or is explicitly revoked.

### REQ-200 — Users authenticate with email and password

- **Priority:** must
- **Status:** implemented
- **Related:** REQ-201, REQ-209
- **Implemented by:** `src/server/services/auth-service.ts` — `login`, `src/server/repositories/user-repository.ts` — `findUserByEmail`
- **Verified by:** `tests/schemas/auth.schema.test.ts`

There is no OAuth, SSO or magic-link path in Taskflow; `login(input)` in `auth-service.ts`
takes an email and password, looks up the user by email
(`user-repository.ts#findUserByEmail`), and verifies the password against the stored hash.
This is a deliberate scope limitation for a product aimed at small-to-mid teams that do not
require enterprise identity federation on day one.

**Acceptance criteria**

1. `loginSchema` requires both an email and a password field; there is no alternate
   credential type accepted.
2. A login attempt against a non-existent email fails with the same generic error a wrong
   password would, avoiding user enumeration through differing error messages.
3. `findUserByEmail` is case-normalized so `User@Example.com` and `user@example.com` resolve
   to the same account.

- **Status:** implemented
- **Related:** ADR-020, REQ-200
- **Implemented by:** `src/lib/hash.ts` — `hashPassword`, `verifyPassword`
- **Verified by:** `tests/lib/hash.test.ts`

external hashing dependency. `insertUser` never receives a plaintext password parameter — its
input type is `{ email: string; name: string; passwordHash: string }`, so a plaintext
password literally cannot reach the repository layer through the type system.

**Acceptance criteria**

1. No repository or schema type includes a plaintext `password` field alongside a stored
   user record; only `passwordHash`.
2. `verifyPassword` performs a comparison resistant to short-circuit timing differences (the
   underlying scrypt-based comparison, not a naive string equality check).
3. `hashPassword`'s output differs between two calls with the same input password, since a
   fresh salt is used each time.

   explicitly excluded from this redirect, since they are the login/register/reset flow
   itself.
3. The redirect preserves the originally requested path so login can return the user to
   where they were headed, where the login form supports it.

### REQ-212 — The request hook rejects requests for unknown organizations

- **Priority:** should
- **Status:** implemented
- **Related:** REQ-002, ADR-007
- **Implemented by:** `src/proxy.ts` — `proxy`, `src/lib/actor.ts` — `getActor`
- **Verified by:** `tests/lib/tenant.test.ts`

Beyond the session check, the proxy (or the page-level `getActor` call it precedes) rejects
requests naming an `orgSlug` that does not resolve to any organization, or that resolves to
one the session's user is not a member of — this is the practical enforcement point for
`REQ-011`'s cross-tenant guard at the routing layer, before any page-specific data fetching
even begins.

**Acceptance criteria**

1. A request to `/nonexistent-slug/...` does not render a dashboard shell before failing;
   it fails at resolution.
2. A request to a real `orgSlug` the current user does not belong to is treated the same as
   a nonexistent slug from the requester's point of view — no information about the
   organization's existence is leaked.
3. This check runs on every dashboard request, not only on the first request after login.

### REQ-213 — A user may belong to several organizations

- **Priority:** must
- **Status:** implemented
- **Related:** REQ-009, REQ-210, DES-041
- **Implemented by:** `src/server/repositories/organization-repository.ts` — `listOrgsForUser`, `src/server/services/organization-service.ts` — `listOrganizationsForUser`
- **Verified by:** none — covered indirectly; see the gaps section of the test plan

`listOrgsForUser(userId)` returns every organization a user is an active member of; there is
no limit on how many organizations one `User` row can belong to, and `user-repository.ts` is
deliberately the one repository not scoped by `orgId`, since a user's identity is global
even though every role they hold is per-organization.

**Acceptance criteria**

1. `listOrganizationsForUser` reflects membership across every organization, including ones
   where the user's role is `viewer`.
2. A user removed from one organization (`REQ-033`) retains full access to their other
   organizations, unaffected.
3. The organization switcher UI is populated from `listOrgsForUser`, not from any cached or
   session-embedded list that could go stale as memberships change.

1	---
2	title: Webhook requirements
3	id: REQ-WEBHOOKS
4	status: approved
5	owners: [product-team, k.ferreira]
6	last_updated: 2026-05-26
7	related: [REQ-136, REQ-152, ADR-018, DES-170]
8	---
9	
10	## Scope
11	
12	This document defines the requirements for webhook endpoint management and outbound delivery:
13	configuration, signing, queuing, batched claiming, retry with backoff, the attempt ceiling,
14	and visibility into delivery history. It does not define the plan quota arithmetic
15	(`billing-and-plan-limits.md`) or the general event catalogue (referenced throughout, defined
16	in `src/types/event.ts`).
17	
18	## Context
19	
20	`webhook-service.ts` manages endpoints (`createWebhook`, `updateWebhook`, `deleteWebhook`,
21	`listWebhooks`) and bridges the event bus to the delivery queue: `registerWebhookListeners`
22	subscribes to `webhook.delivery_requested` and calls
23	`webhook-repository.ts#enqueueDelivery` for every active endpoint subscribed to that event
24	type. Endpoint rows and delivery-attempt rows live in
25	`src/server/repositories/webhook-repository.ts`; delivery itself never happens inline with
26	the request that produced the triggering event (`REQ-154`) — it is always a queue-and-drain
27	pattern consumed by `webhook-delivery-job.ts` on its own cadence.
28	
29	`ADR-018` documents the decision to queue deliveries with capped exponential backoff instead
30	of the simpler inline-delivery approach `ADR-005` originally sketched for the event bus in
31	general: webhook endpoints are third-party HTTP servers outside Taskflow's control, and a
32	slow or down endpoint cannot be allowed to block the request that triggered the event, or to
33	retry synchronously inside that request's lifetime. `runWebhookDeliveryJob(now)` runs on the
34	`webhook-delivery` cadence — every 1 minute, the tightest cadence of any job, chosen because
35	webhook consumers (billing systems, chat integrations, CI triggers) are often time-sensitive.
36	
37	Each delivery attempt claims a bounded batch (`CLAIM_BATCH = 25`) via
38	`claimPendingDeliveries(limit)`, so one job tick cannot try to drain an unbounded backlog in
39	one pass and risk starving other organizations' deliveries if one org has a large pending
40	queue. A delivery is abandoned after `MAX_ATTEMPTS = 6` failed tries, with `backoffMs()`
41	computing 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, 32s — doubling each attempt, capped at 300000 ms (5 minutes)
42	— though in practice six attempts at doubling delay from a 1-minute-cadence job never
43	actually reaches the cap; the cap exists as a safety bound for any future change to the
44	attempt count or cadence, not because the current numbers require it.
45	
46	Every endpoint holds a secret (`REQ-153`) used by `signPayload(secret, payload)` in
47	`webhook-service.ts` to HMAC-sign the outgoing body, letting the receiving server verify
48	the request actually came from Taskflow and was not forged or tampered with in transit.
49	
50	Delivery is deliberately fire-and-forget from the perspective of the domain service that
51	triggered the underlying event: `issue-service.ts`, `comment-service.ts` and the rest never
52	learn whether a webhook delivery eventually succeeded, failed, or was abandoned after six
53	attempts. That feedback loop exists only inside the settings UI (`REQ-159`), which is a
54	conscious layering choice — coupling issue or comment mutation logic to webhook delivery
55	outcomes would reintroduce exactly the kind of cross-cutting dependency `ADR-005`'s
56	in-process event bus was designed to avoid, at the cost of making delivery failures a
57	"go check the settings page" concern rather than something that surfaces automatically to
58	the person who took the original action.
59	
60	## Open questions
61	
62	1. `REQ-159` says delivery attempts are visible in the settings UI, but this document does
63	   not specify a retention policy for delivery-attempt rows distinct from the organization's
64	   general `retentionDays` — whether stale delivery history for a long-lived endpoint grows
65	   unbounded is not addressed by any requirement here.
66	2. `REQ-157`'s abandonment after six attempts has no requirement describing whether the
67	   endpoint owner is notified of the abandonment, versus only being able to discover it by
68	   checking the delivery-attempts UI.
69	3. Whether re-enabling a previously disabled endpoint (`REQ-158`) should retry deliveries
70	   that were fast-failed while it was disabled, or whether those are permanently lost, is
71	   unresolved.
72	4. `REQ-161`'s per-org delivery rate limit and `REQ-155`'s per-tick claim batch interact in
73	   a way no requirement fully specifies: a burst well within the claim batch but above the
74	   rate-limit bucket defers to a later tick, but nothing here says how many ticks a
75	   deferred-but-not-failed delivery may accumulate before it is effectively starved out by
76	   newer events from the same organization repeatedly winning the claim.
77	
78	### REQ-150 — Webhook endpoints are configured per organization
79	
80	- **Priority:** must
81	- **Status:** implemented
82	- **Related:** REQ-010, REQ-136
83	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/repositories/webhook-repository.ts` — `listEndpoints`, `src/server/services/webhook-service.ts` — `createWebhook`
84	- **Verified by:** none — covered indirectly; see the gaps section of the test plan
85	
86	`webhook-repository.ts`'s endpoint table carries `org_id`; `listEndpoints(orgId)` and every
87	other function scope strictly to one organization, matching the tenancy discipline every
88	other domain follows. There is no shared or platform-level webhook endpoint that spans
89	organizations.
90	
91	**Acceptance criteria**
92	
93	1. `listEndpoints` never returns another organization's endpoints.
94	2. `createWebhook`'s input is validated against `src/schemas/webhook.ts` and always carries
95	   the actor's `orgId`, never a client-supplied one.
96	3. Deleting an organization (soft delete, `REQ-007`) does not delete its webhook endpoints
97	   outright, consistent with the archive-not-delete pattern, but active delivery for an
98	   archived org's endpoints should not continue — see `REQ-158`'s disabled-fast-fail path as
99	   the closest existing mechanism.
100	
101	### REQ-151 — Endpoint management requires admin
102	
103	- **Priority:** must
104	- **Status:** implemented
105	- **Related:** REQ-024, ADR-003
106	- **Implemented by:** `src/lib/permissions.ts` — `ROLE_MATRIX`
107	- **Verified by:** `tests/lib/permissions.matrix.test.ts`
108	
109	`webhook:manage`'s `ROLE_MATRIX` minimum is `admin`; there is no ownership escalation for
110	webhook endpoints the way there is for issues and comments, since an endpoint is
111	organization infrastructure, not personally authored content — every admin can manage every
112	endpoint equally, with no notion of "the admin who created it" having special standing.
113	
114	**Acceptance criteria**
115	
116	1. A `member` cannot call `createWebhookAction`, `updateWebhookAction` or
117	   `deleteWebhookAction` regardless of any relationship to the endpoint.
118	2. `webhook:manage` does not appear in the ownership-escalation action list in
119	   `src/lib/permissions.ts`.
120	3. Any `admin` in the org, not only the endpoint's creator, can delete or update it.
121	
122	### REQ-152 — Webhooks require a plan that includes them
123	
124	- **Priority:** must
125	- **Status:** implemented
126	- **Related:** REQ-136, REQ-188, ADR-012
127	- **Implemented by:** `src/lib/feature-flags.ts` — `isEnabled`, `src/server/services/webhook-service.ts` — `createWebhook`
128	- **Verified by:** `tests/lib/feature-flags.test.ts`
129	
130	The `webhooks` feature flag (`growth` plan minimum, **not** overridable, per the product
131	facts) gates both endpoint creation and delivery — unlike most flags, `webhooks` cannot be
132	turned on early for a `starter` org via an org-level override, which is a deliberate
133	restriction distinct from the endpoint-count quota in `REQ-136`.
134	
135	**Acceptance criteria**
136	
137	1. `createWebhookAction` on a `free` or `starter` org without the flag returns
138	   `FeatureDisabledError`/`feature_disabled`, independent of the count-based quota check.
139	2. An org-level override attempting to force `webhooks` on below `growth` has no effect,
140	   since the flag definition marks it non-overridable.
141	3. `runWebhookDeliveryJob` skips delivery for any endpoint belonging to an org whose current
142	   plan no longer includes the flag (a downgrade case), even if the endpoint row itself
143	   still exists.
144	
145	### REQ-153 — Each endpoint holds a secret used to sign payloads
146	
147	- **Priority:** must
148	- **Status:** implemented
149	- **Related:** REQ-160, DES-180
150	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/repositories/webhook-repository.ts` — `insertEndpoint`, `src/server/services/webhook-service.ts` — `signPayload`
151	- **Verified by:** none — covered indirectly; see the gaps section of the test plan
152	
153	`insertEndpoint(input, secret)` stores a per-endpoint secret generated at creation;
154	`signPayload(secret, payload)` HMAC-signs the serialized delivery body, and the signature is
155	sent alongside the payload so the receiving server can verify authenticity. The secret is
156	never re-derivable from the signature; it is a shared value fixed at endpoint creation and
157	rotatable only by recreating the endpoint (there is no `rotateSecret` in the manifest).
158	
159	**Acceptance criteria**
160	
161	1. Two endpoints, even for the same organization, receive independently generated secrets.
162	2. `signPayload` produces a deterministic signature for a given secret and payload, so the
163	   receiving server's own recomputation matches.
164	3. The secret is never included in `listWebhooks`'s response shown to the settings UI in
165	   plaintext after initial creation (only surfaced once, at creation time, if at all,
166	   matching the general practice for credential-like values).
167	
168	### REQ-154 — Deliveries are queued, never sent inline with a request
169	
170	- **Priority:** must
171	- **Status:** implemented
172	- **Related:** ADR-018, ADR-005
173	
174	`registerWebhookListeners`'s handler for `webhook.delivery_requested` only calls
175	`enqueueDelivery`; it never performs the outbound HTTP call itself. This decouples the
176	request that triggered the underlying domain event (an issue status change, say) from the
177	health and latency of a third-party webhook receiver.
178	
179	**Acceptance criteria**
180	
181	1. No code path between an original domain-event emission and `enqueueDelivery` performs
182	   network I/O.
183	2. A Server Action that triggers a webhook-eligible event returns to its caller without
184	   waiting for any webhook delivery attempt.
185	3. `enqueueDelivery`'s write happens synchronously within request handling; only the actual
186	   HTTP delivery is deferred to the job.
187	
188	**Implemented by:** `src/server/services/webhook-service.ts`, `src/server/repositories/webhook-repository.ts`
189	**Verified by:** `tests/server/jobs.test.ts`
190	
191	### REQ-155 — Deliveries are claimed in bounded batches
192	
193	- **Priority:** must
194	- **Status:** implemented
195	- **Related:** REQ-154, ADR-018
196	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/repositories/webhook-repository.ts` — `claimPendingDeliveries`
197	- **Verified by:** `tests/server/jobs.test.ts`
198	
199	`CLAIM_BATCH = 25` bounds how many pending deliveries `claimPendingDeliveries(limit)`
200	returns to one job tick, preventing a large backlog for one organization from starving
201	delivery attempts for every other organization's endpoints in the same tick, given the job
202	runs across all organizations rather than per-org.
203	
204	**Acceptance criteria**
205	
206	1. `claimPendingDeliveries` never returns more than `CLAIM_BATCH` rows in one call.
207	2. A claimed delivery is not claimable again by a concurrent tick until it is marked
208	   delivered, failed, or its claim expires.
209	3. An organization with a delivery backlog larger than `CLAIM_BATCH` has its remaining
210	   deliveries picked up on subsequent ticks, not dropped.
211	
212	### REQ-156 — Failed deliveries retry with exponential backoff
213	
214	- **Priority:** must
215	- **Status:** implemented
216	- **Related:** REQ-157, ADR-018
217	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/jobs/webhook-delivery-job.ts` — `backoffMs`, `runWebhookDeliveryJob`
218	- **Verified by:** `tests/server/jobs.test.ts`
219	
220	`backoffMs(attempts)` in `webhook-delivery-job.ts` returns 1000, 2000, 4000ms and so on,
221	doubling per attempt and capped at 300000 ms. A failed delivery is not retried immediately
222	within the same tick; `markDeliveryFailed` records the failure and the next eligible attempt
223	waits at least `backoffMs(attempts)` before becoming claimable again.
224	
225	**Acceptance criteria**
226	
227	1. `backoffMs(1)` is 1000; `backoffMs(2)` is 2000; the sequence doubles until the 300000 ms
228	   cap.
229	2. A delivery is not reclaimed by `claimPendingDeliveries` before its backoff interval has
230	   elapsed since the last failed attempt.
231	3. `backoffMs` never returns a value exceeding 300000, regardless of how high `attempts`
232	   grows.
233	
234	### REQ-157 — A delivery is abandoned after a fixed attempt ceiling
235	
236	- **Priority:** must
237	- **Status:** implemented
238	- **Related:** REQ-156, DES-180
239	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/jobs/webhook-delivery-job.ts` — `runWebhookDeliveryJob`, `src/config/constants.ts` — `WEBHOOK_MAX_ATTEMPTS`
240	- **Verified by:** `tests/server/jobs.test.ts`
241	
242	`MAX_ATTEMPTS = 6`. Once a delivery's attempt count reaches this ceiling without a
243	successful response, it is no longer retried; it stays in a terminal failed state, visible
244	through the delivery-attempts UI (`REQ-159`) but no longer occupying the retry queue.
245	
246	**Acceptance criteria**
247	
248	1. A delivery's seventh attempt never happens; the sixth failure is terminal.
249	2. The terminal state is distinguishable in the delivery-attempts UI from an in-progress
250	   retry, so an operator can tell "still trying" from "gave up."
251	3. `MAX_ATTEMPTS` is read from `WEBHOOK_MAX_ATTEMPTS` in `src/config/constants.ts`, not
252	   hardcoded separately in `webhook-delivery-job.ts`.
253	
254	### REQ-158 — Deliveries to a disabled endpoint fail fast
255	
256	- **Priority:** should
257	- **Status:** implemented
258	- **Related:** REQ-136, REQ-152
259	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/jobs/webhook-delivery-job.ts` — `runWebhookDeliveryJob`
260	- **Verified by:** `tests/server/jobs.test.ts`
261	
262	An endpoint can be toggled disabled without being deleted; a delivery targeting a disabled
263	endpoint is marked failed immediately by the job, without consuming an HTTP round trip or
264	counting toward the meaningful part of the attempt budget the way a genuine network failure
265	would, since the failure here is a known local condition, not the endpoint's own health.
266	
267	**Acceptance criteria**
268	
269	1. `runWebhookDeliveryJob` checks the endpoint's enabled state before attempting the HTTP
270	   call, not after a failed attempt.
271	2. A disabled endpoint's pending deliveries are marked failed without incrementing latency
272	   metrics an actual network call would produce.
273	3. Re-enabling the endpoint allows new deliveries (from new events) to queue and attempt
274	   normally; whether previously fast-failed deliveries are retried is the open question
275	   noted above.
276	
277	### REQ-159 — Delivery attempts are visible in the settings UI
278	
279	- **Priority:** should
280	- **Status:** implemented
281	- **Related:** REQ-157, DES-190
282	- **Implemented by:** `src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/settings/webhooks/webhook-manager.tsx`, `src/server/repositories/webhook-repository.ts` — `markDelivered`, `markDeliveryFailed`
283	- **Verified by:** none — covered indirectly; see the gaps section of the test plan
284	
285	`src/app/(dashboard)/[orgSlug]/settings/webhooks/webhook-manager.tsx` renders each
286	endpoint's recent delivery attempts, backed by the delivery-attempt rows
287	`webhook-repository.ts` maintains alongside `markDelivered`/`markDeliveryFailed`, giving an
288	admin visibility into whether their integration is actually receiving events without needing
289	to inspect logs outside the product.
290	
291	**Acceptance criteria**
292	
293	1. The webhook settings page shows, at minimum, delivery status, attempt count and last
294	   attempt time per endpoint.
295	2. A terminally failed delivery (`REQ-157`) is visually distinguishable from one still
296	   retrying.
297	3. The list only shows the requesting organization's own endpoints and their own deliveries.
298	
299	### REQ-160 — Webhook payloads carry the event type and envelope
300	
301	- **Priority:** must
302	- **Status:** implemented
303	- **Related:** REQ-153, DES-071
304	- **Implemented by:** `src/server/repositories/webhook-repository.ts` — `enqueueDelivery`
305	- **Verified by:** `tests/server/jobs.test.ts`
306	
307	Every delivered payload includes the originating event's type string (one of the 21 keys in
308	`TaskflowEventMap`) and the standard `EventEnvelope` fields (`orgId`, `actorId`,
309	`occurredAt`), so a receiving integration can dispatch on event type without needing a
310	Taskflow-specific schema per event beyond what the envelope already standardizes.
311
